title: RC Charging: Why a Capacitor Fills on an Exponential Curve
topic: RC charging transient — a battery, resistor and capacitor in series; after the switch closes the capacitor voltage rises as V_C(t) = V_0(1 − e^{−t/τ}); the time constant τ = RC sets the speed (63% at one τ, ≈99% after five τ)

beats.narration: Close a switch and a capacitor starts filling — how fast does it get there?

elements.content: Switch closes — how fast does the capacitor fill?

beats.narration: Battery V zero in series with a resistor R and capacitor C. Flip the switch, and current starts pushing charge onto the plates.

elements.content: Series loop: battery V0 on the left, switch closing in the top branch, resistor R, capacitor C on the right side
Current-flow dots travelling clockwise around the loop once the switch closes
current rushes in, then slows as the cap fills

beats.narration: The voltage across the capacitor climbs along an exponential curve — V of t equals V zero times one minus e to the minus t over tau.

elements.content: t (horizontal) vs V_C (vertical), 0 to 5τ on t, 0 to V₀ on V
Exponential approach to V₀, traced left to right as the time cursor sweeps
Capacitor symbol on the right — top plate fills with positive charge dots, bottom plate accumulates negative charges as the curve traces

beats.narration: Tau equals R times C is the time constant. After one tau the voltage has reached sixty three percent. After five tau it is essentially full.

elements.content: one τ → 63%   ·   five τ → essentially full

beats.narration: Bigger R or bigger C means slower charging. The time constant R times C sets the entire rhythm.

elements.content: Bigger R or bigger C → slower charge.
